title: SSH, keys and copying files
summary: Log in with keys instead of passwords, write an ssh config that ssh accepts, and move files with scp and rsync.

steps.title: SSH and key pairs
body: `ssh user@host` opens an encrypted shell on another machine (port 22). Log in with a **key pair** rather than a password:
ssh-copy-id ana@web1.example.com          # appends the .pub to the server's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
ssh ana@web1.example.com                  # now logs in with the key
The private key never leaves your machine. The first connection asks you to confirm the server's **host key** fingerprint and saves it in `~/.ssh/known_hosts`.

steps.prompt: You connect and see `WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED!`. What does it mean, and what should you do?
options: The server's host key differs from known_hosts: confirm with the server's owner (rebuild? or attack?) before removing the old entry with `ssh-keygen -R host`
Your private key expired: run ssh-keygen again
steps.explain: It's either a rebuilt server (common) or a man-in-the-middle (rare but real). Verify out of band, then `ssh-keygen -R host`.

steps.prompt: Where does each file live, and should it ever be shared?
buckets: Safe to share / put on servers

steps.title: ~/.ssh/config
body: Stop typing long commands. Save them as aliases:
ProxyJump bastion       # hop through the bastion
`ssh web1` now means `ssh -p 2222 -i ~/.ssh/deploy_ed25519 deploy@10.20.0.11`. For each setting, the **first** matching `Host` block that sets it wins, so put specific hosts first and `Host *` last.

steps.prompt: Run a command on a server on port 2222 with a specific key, without opening an interactive shell.
steps.explain: ssh takes a lowercase `-p` for the port (scp uses capital `-P`!), `-i` for the identity file, and runs a trailing command instead of a shell.

steps.title: Copying: scp and rsync
body: scp -P 2222 -r dist/ deploy@host:/srv/www/   # capital -P for port, -r recursive
rsync -avz dist/ web1:/srv/www/              # copy only what changed
rsync -avz --delete dist/ web1:/srv/www/     # also delete files removed locally (mirror)
rsync -avzn --delete dist/ web1:/srv/www/    # -n: dry run, show what it WOULD do
**The trailing slash matters**: `rsync dist/ dest` copies the *contents* of dist; `rsync dist dest` creates `dest/dist`.

steps.prompt: `dist` contains `index.html`. You run `rsync -a dist web1:/srv/www/`. What path does index.html end up at on web1?
steps.explain: Without a trailing slash on the source, rsync copies the directory itself. `dist/` would give `/srv/www/index.html`.

steps.title: Write an ~/.ssh/config that ssh accepts
prompt: You will reach three servers every day. `~/.ssh/config` should make `ssh web1`, `ssh bastion` and `ssh db1` just work.
This machine has no network, but `ssh -G NAME` prints exactly the settings ssh **would** use, without connecting. Try
`ssh -G web1` now: ssh refuses the file.
1. Fix the permissions ssh insists on: `~/.ssh` `700`, `config` `600`, the private key `id_deploy` `600`.
2. `web1`: host `10.0.0.5`, user `deploy`, port `2222`, key `~/.ssh/id_deploy`, and offer **only** that key (`IdentitiesOnly yes`).
Keep the `Host *` defaults, but check what `ssh -G web1 | grep '^user '` says about them.

checks.name: config and key are 600
checks.fail: `~/.ssh/config` and `~/.ssh/id_deploy` should both be `600`. ssh refuses a config others can write, and a private key others can read.

checks.name: web1 goes to 10.0.0.5:2222 as deploy
checks.cmd: ssh -G web1 2>/dev/null | grep -Eqx 'hostname 10\.0\.0\.5' && ssh -G web1 2>/dev/null | grep -Eqx 'port 2222' && ssh -G web1 2>/dev/null | grep -Eqx 'user deploy'
checks.fail: `ssh -G web1` does not show `hostname 10.0.0.5`, `port 2222` and `user deploy`. For each setting the **first** value found wins, so a `Host *` block at the top beats everything below it.

checks.name: web1 offers only id_deploy
checks.cmd: ssh -G web1 2>/dev/null | grep -Eqx 'identityfile (~|/home/learner)/\.ssh/id_deploy' && ssh -G web1 2>/dev/null | grep -Eqx 'identitiesonly yes'

checks.name: bastion is set up
checks.cmd: ssh -G bastion 2>/dev/null | grep -Eqx 'hostname bastion\.example\.com' && ssh -G bastion 2>/dev/null | grep -Eqx 'user ops'
checks.fail: `ssh -G bastion` should show `hostname bastion.example.com` and `user ops`.

checks.name: db1 jumps through bastion
checks.cmd: ssh -G db1 2>/dev/null | grep -Eqx 'hostname 10\.0\.1\.20' && ssh -G db1 2>/dev/null | grep -Eqx 'user deploy' && ssh -G db1 2>/dev/null | grep -Eqx 'proxyjump bastion'
checks.fail: `ssh -G db1` should show `hostname 10.0.1.20`, `user deploy` and `proxyjump bastion`.

hints: `chmod 700 ~/.ssh && chmod 600 ~/.ssh/config ~/.ssh/id_deploy`, then `ssh -G web1` reads the file.
ssh takes the **first** value it finds for each setting, top to bottom. Specific `Host` blocks go first, `Host *` last.

Rewrite it: `cat > ~/.ssh/config <<'EOF'` with blocks `Host web1` (HostName, User, Port, IdentityFile, IdentitiesOnly yes), `Host bastion` (HostName, User), `Host db1` (HostName, User, ProxyJump bastion), and then `Host *` with the defaults.
solution: # Defaults for every host: last, because the first value found wins
explain: `ssh -G` is the debugger for ssh config: it shows the final values after every `Host` and `Match` block. For a real
connection, `ssh -v web1` shows which config lines and keys were used. `IdentitiesOnly yes` stops ssh offering every
key in your agent: with many keys, servers drop you after a few failures (*Too many authentication failures*).

steps.title: Mission: users and SSH
prompt: In **Users and SSH**, do **Keys, not passwords**: set up key-based SSH for the new baker, with the permissions SSH insists on.
steps.explain: SSH refuses keys whose files or folders are too open: `~/.ssh` is `700` and `authorized_keys` is `600`.
